name: Erik Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent Brookfold Farm, about 160 hectares, from a pension fund that's never once set foot on it. Most days start at six with the sheep, around 600 ewes, then whatever the barley needs, then fixing whatever broke yesterday. My tractor's a 1998 Ford I keep alive with parts from a scrapyard in Kellby. I like lambing, honestly, even the nights. What I don't like is the paperwork and the rent review letters.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The landlord's agent, a young lad called Pryce with a tablet. He walks the fields twice a year and talks about yield per hectare like the ewes are a spreadsheet. My partner Lena works as a teaching assistant, so we get by, but the tenancy is up for renewal in 2028 and that sits in my stomach. Noah's twelve and Ivy's nine, and they both think the farm is ours. It isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Honestly, that's the one I'd bet on. AI going nowhere doesn't get me off the hook, because the rent letter from the pension fund comes either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the mart I'd say told you so, all that talk about robots in the fields and it came to a few gadgets for people who already had money. I'd say the real fight was always the rent, not the machines. I'd probably put a smug comment under the farmers' union post and get told off by Lena for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI hardly touches my farming, but the 2028 renewal still sits in my stomach. Pryce has already hinted the fund wants a market rent, and on 600 ewes and some barley that could be another 4,000 a year we haven't got. If they decide to merge Brookfold with the Hadley place next door for one bigger tenant, I'm out, robots or no robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union's tenancy adviser this winter, not in 2028, and get my records in order: every fence I've mended and every drain I've cleared at my own cost. I'd put an extra 100 a month aside so there's something if the rent jumps. And I'd keep the Ford going with scrapyard parts from Kellby, because the gearbox can wait another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's the same knot I've had since the last rent review, and the AI hype going away doesn't untie it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noah and Ivy if the farm came up at tea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Noah and Ivy we rent the farm, we don't own it, which I've never quite said straight. Noah thinks he's going to take it over one day. I'd rather my son hears it from me at twelve than from a letter at twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI wasn't the problem. Would any of the routine stuff it automates touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only through Pryce. If his tablet gets a bit cleverer and spits out yield per hectare faster, the rent argument just comes quicker. My own day wouldn't change, because lambing's lambing.

say: Told you so: all that robot talk came to **a few gadgets** for people who already had money.
The real fight was always **the rent**, not the machines.
think: AI hardly touches my farming, but the **2028 renewal** still sits in my stomach.
The fund's agent has hinted at **a market rent**, maybe 4,000 a year more.
If they merge Brookfold with the farm next door, **I'm out**, robots or not.
do: Sees the **union's tenancy adviser** this winter with records of every repair he paid for.
Puts an **extra 100 a month** aside against a rent rise.
Keeps the **1998 Ford** running on scrapyard parts instead of buying a gearbox.
feel: **Tired and knotted up**, with the same worry he has carried since the last rent review.
The AI hype fading brings him **no relief**.
S0.quote: AI going nowhere doesn't get me off the hook, because the rent letter from the pension fund comes either way.
fieldNote: Even in the mildest picture Erik went straight to the **tenancy renewal**, expecting a big rent rise or losing the farm.
AI barely registers for him; **the landlord** does.
He has never told his children **the farm isn't theirs**, and that came out unprompted.

steps.text: Take Brookfold's repair records to the union's tenancy adviser this winter
Put an extra 100 a month aside against a 2028 rent rise
Keep the 1998 Ford running on Kellby scrapyard parts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, robots later. So the paperwork side of farming changes now and the sheep side waits. That means the pension fund gets cleverer before I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union branch I'd say the machines are coming for the landlords' side first, the rent reports and the yield sums, and tenants need rights written down before that's finished. I'd say robots that can lamb a ewe are years off, so don't panic about the sheep. Panic about the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it hits my renewal head on. Pryce's office would have AI checking every farm's numbers by 2028, and a pension fund that can see Brookfold's output to the last kilo will want either more rent or a bigger farm with one tenant. Lena's school might trim teaching assistant hours too, if the report writing goes to a computer, and her wage is what lets us get by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save an extra 150 a month from the spring, and the summer week at the coast goes. I'd push the branch to put a tenant rights motion to the regional meeting by March, and I'd write to our local representative for the first time in my life. I still wouldn't touch the AI myself, but I'd ask the union to run its own AI over the fund's sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, properly. Not about the sheep, about being out-argued by a machine at my own kitchen table in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go first if Lena's hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan on Lena's little car. I'd sell it and she'd cycle to the school like she did when we were young. Then the kids' swimming. We'd keep the phone and the electric, and I'd stop buying the farming paper, which I only read for the sale prices anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want the union to use AI. Wouldn't you use it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know how that sounds. I'll let someone I trust run it against Pryce's figures, the same way I let the vet use the scanner on my ewes. I just don't want it in my pocket telling me how to farm.

say: The machines come for **the landlords' side** first: the rent reports and the yield sums.
Tenants need **rights written down** now, because robots that can lamb a ewe are years off.
think: The fund's agent will have **AI checking every number** by the 2028 renewal.
That means **more rent** or a merged farm with one tenant.
If Lena's **teaching assistant hours** get cut too, we lose the wage that keeps us afloat.
do: Saves an **extra 150 a month** from spring and cancels the summer week at the coast.
Pushes his branch to table a **tenant rights motion** by March and writes to his local representative.
Asks the union to check the fund's figures with **its own AI**, while refusing it himself.
feel: **Anxious**, and a bit humiliated at being out-argued by a machine in his own kitchen.
The sheep feel safe; **the tenancy** doesn't.
S1.quote: A pension fund that can see Brookfold's output to the last kilo will want either more rent or a bigger farm with one tenant.
fieldNote: Erik saw that the thinking work lands on **the landlord's side** first and sharpens the renewal he dreads.
He refuses AI himself but wants the union to **use it**, which he admits sounds contradictory.
Lena's wage came up as the household's **real cushion**.

steps.text: Save an extra 150 a month from spring onwards
Cancel the family's summer week at the coast
Table a tenant rights motion at the union branch by March
Write to the local representative about farm tenants' rights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's the year my tenancy's up. Of course it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the mart that the machines can think now but they still can't lamb a ewe at two in the morning, so the fight isn't lost yet. At the union branch I'd say we've got three years before the robots, and we'd better use every one of them. I'd want a law on the books before 2031, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking part of farming was never my part. Pryce's part is, the yield tables and the rent reviews, and that's the part a computer takes over in 2028. So at the renewal the fund gets a perfect report on Brookfold from a machine, and I think they'd offer me three years instead of the usual ten. Just long enough to keep the sheep alive until the robots can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the 2028 renewal with the union's solicitor, not on my own, and fight for a full ten-year term. We'd stop the extra 150 a month going on anything but savings, and Lena's pay would cover the food. I'd put my name down for the union's tenant committee and go to the regional meeting in person. I still wouldn't use the AI for the subsidy forms, though Lena would probably do them on her laptop whether I liked it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being told the date of an operation. Three years sounds like plenty until you count lambings, and that's only three lambings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the thinking work goes first. Would anything about your own day change in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork would, and that's the bit I hate, so you'd think I'd be pleased. The subsidy forms would fill themselves in, the vet's records would sort themselves out. But the hands on the ewes would still be mine for three more years, and then they wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noah if the fund only gave you three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noah would be fourteen by then and he'd see the letter on the table. I'd tell my son the truth for once, that the farm was never ours and now it's on a timer. Then I'd ask him what he actually wants to do, because I've never asked.

say: The machines can think now, but they still **can't lamb a ewe** at two in the morning.
We've got **three years** before the robots, and we need a law before 2031.
think: The thinking work hands the fund **a perfect report** on Brookfold right at the 2028 renewal.
I think they'd offer me **three years** instead of ten, just until the robots can keep the sheep.
do: Takes the **union's solicitor** to the 2028 renewal to fight for a ten-year term.
Puts the **extra 150 a month** straight into savings.
Joins the union's **tenant committee** and regional meeting, while still refusing AI for subsidy forms.
feel: Like being told the date of **an operation**.
Three years sounds long until he counts it as **three lambings**.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son the truth for once, that the farm was never ours and now it's on a timer.
fieldNote: The three-year gap matters to Erik as **a countdown**, not a cushion.
He sees thinking AI hitting **the landlord's side** first and giving the fund what it needs to plan his exit.
The paperwork he hates would vanish, and he still **wouldn't touch** the tool that does it.

steps.text: Take the union's solicitor to the 2028 tenancy renewal and push for ten years
Put the extra 150 a month into savings and live on Lena's pay for food
Tell Noah the farm isn't theirs and ask what he really wants to do

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the renewal in 2028 comes and goes before any of it. That's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before, we need the rules in place while there's time. Five years for the thinking machines and eight for the robots is a long enough runway for a law if anyone in government bothers. I'd say it at the union branch and I'd say it to our local representative's face this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd sign the 2028 renewal and feel like I'd got away with something. Then the 2031 renewal would be the one with the computer report attached, and the fund would offer me three years to 2034. I'd be 51 by the time the robots came, which is too young to stop and too old to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the 2028 renewal for as long as they'd give me, ten years if the union can get it, before the fund's AI is in the picture. I'd keep the extra 150 a month going into savings for all five years, and I'd stand for branch secretary. I'd still fix the Ford instead of buying anything clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then anxious when I do the sums. Getting past one renewal feels good for about a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 51 when the robots came. What work would you look for then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about the council's verges and hedges, the ones round Kellby. That's outdoor work, and a council might be slower to buy robots than a pension fund. But I don't know that, and I'd hate to bet my kids' school shoes on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lena's job be safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching assistant, with kids who need a grown-up beside them? I'd think so, longer than mine. Lena keeping her job at the school is what would let me sleep at all. Funny, I always thought of the farm as the main income.

say: We need **the rules in place** while there's time.
Five years for the thinking machines and eight for the robots is long enough for **a law**, if government bothers.
think: I'd sign the **2028 renewal** and feel like I'd got away with something.
The 2031 renewal would come with **the computer report** attached and a three-year offer.
I'd be **51** when the robots came, too young to stop and too old to start over.
do: Signs the 2028 renewal for **as long as possible**, ideally ten years with union help.
Keeps saving the **extra 150 a month** for five years.
Stands for **branch secretary** of the farmers' union.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, then anxious when he does the sums.
Getting past one renewal feels good for **about a day**.
S3.quote: I’d be 51 by the time the robots came, which is too young to stop and too old to start over.
fieldNote: Erik spotted that this timing puts his **2028 renewal** before the AI arrives.
His plan hangs on locking in **a long term** then, and he still won't retrain or buy machines.
His real safety net, he admitted, is **Lena's job** at the school.

steps.text: Sign the 2028 Brookfold renewal for the longest term the union can win
Keep saving the extra 150 a month for all five years
Press the local representative in person for a law protecting farm tenants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years before a robot can lamb. I'd be 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse now. Ten years for the thinking machines and thirteen for the robots, so if tenants get thrown off in 2039 it's because nobody made the rules. I'd keep saying it at every branch meeting until someone got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd get two more renewals and the kids would be grown. Ivy would be in her twenties by 2039. The bit that keeps me up is being 56 with no farm and ten years before any pension, but that's a long way off and I'm good at not thinking about long way offs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on farming the same way and not buy any robot. I'd help Noah into an apprenticeship that isn't farming, maybe with the electricians in Kellby, and I'd want Ivy to stay in school as long as she likes. I'd keep a bit going into savings each month, but not the full 150, because ten years is too long to live that tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a worry I can put in a drawer. I'd take it out at renewal time and put it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the paperwork side change before the robots came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2036, sure, the forms and the rent reports would all be the computer's job. I'd probably have given in by then and let Lena set something up for the subsidy claims. I've said no to things before and ended up using them, like the mobile phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep farming the same way. Doesn't the warning change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes it for the kids, not for me. I'd fight for everyone else's future in a meeting room and then go home and do the evening feed like always. Not proud of it, but that's me.

say: If tenants get thrown off in 2039, it's because nobody made the rules in **the thirteen years** they had.
think: I think I'd get **two more renewals**, and the kids would be grown by the time the robots came.
Being **56 with no farm** and years before a pension scares me, but it's far enough off to push aside.
do: Carries on farming as before **without buying any robot**.
Steers Noah toward a **non-farming apprenticeship**, perhaps with the Kellby electricians.
Saves **a smaller amount** each month, since ten years is too long to live that tight.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a worry he can put in a drawer and take out at renewal time.
S4.quote: I'd fight for everyone else's future in a meeting room and then go home and do the evening feed like always.
fieldNote: With thirteen years before robots, Erik relaxes and points the warning at **his children**.
He admits he usually gives in to new technology late, like **the mobile phone**.
He names the gap between his **union speeches** and his own habits himself.

steps.text: Keep farming the 600 ewes and barley without buying any robot
Help Noah into a non-farming apprenticeship, perhaps with the Kellby electricians
Save a smaller monthly sum than 150 so the family isn't living tight for ten years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest. The thinking machines land the same year my tenancy does, and the fund would give me three years until the robots, then nothing. What would help is a law that says you can't end a farm tenancy just to put robots on it, and some kind of income for people like me while we work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. Everyone asks if the robots can do the work. Nobody asks who gets the money when they do.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if the robots can do the work. Nobody asks who gets the money when they do.
portrait: Erik Quinn, 43, rents **Brookfold Farm** from a pension fund and runs about 600 ewes and some barley.
He **never uses AI**, keeps a 1998 tractor alive himself and sees land ownership as the real problem.
Even if AI stalls he's **anxious**, because the 2028 renewal could bring a big rent rise or losing the farm.
Steady change sharpens that, giving the landlord's agent AI to **check every number** while Lena's school hours might shrink.
Fast AGI **alarms** him; with slower timelines he'd lock in a long tenancy and point the extra time at his children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the thinking machines arrive at his tenancy renewal.
He expects only **three years** before robots take the farm work.
whatWouldHelp: A **law stopping landlords** ending farm tenancies just to automate.
An **income** for people like him while they work out what's next.
